Mnemonics & Memory Tricks

Who dissolves in excess NaOH?
A–Z
A = Al³⁺ Z = Zn²⁺
"A to Z" — Al³⁺ and Zn²⁺ give a white ppt that dissolves in excess NaOH to form a colourless solution. Every other hydroxide stays insoluble in excess NaOH.
Who dissolves in excess NH₃?
ZnCu
Zn²⁺ → colourless Cu²⁺ → DARK BLUE
"Zoo Creatures dissolve" — Only Zn²⁺ and Cu²⁺ dissolve in excess NH₃. Cu²⁺ gives a stunning DARK BLUE solution — easiest to spot!
Coloured precipitates (not white)
GRB
G = Fe²⁺ (Green) R = Fe³⁺ (Red-brown) B = Cu²⁺ (Light blue)
"Get Rusty Blue" — Fe²⁺ is Green (young iron), Fe³⁺ is Red-Brown (rusty iron), Cu²⁺ is Light Blue. Everything else is WHITE.
Ca²⁺ is the odd one out
Ca = NaOH ONLY
White ppt with NaOH ✓ No ppt with NH₃ ✗
Calcium is "fussy" — it only reacts with NaOH, not NH₃. Use this to distinguish Ca²⁺ from the other white-ppt ions.
NH₄⁺ is special — no precipitate!
NH₄⁺ → GAS
NaOH + warm → NH₃ gas Turns moist red litmus BLUE
"Ammonium doesn't precipitate — it evaporates!" Add NaOH and warm. Colourless, pungent gas turns moist red litmus paper blue = NH₄⁺ confirmed.
Gas Tests — 3 pairs
Splint · Litmus · Bubble
H₂ = lighted splint, POP O₂ = glowing splint relights NH₃ = red litmus → blue Cl₂ = blue litmus → red, bleached CO₂ = limewater white ppt SO₂ = KMnO₄ purple → colourless
Think of gas tests as 3 pairs: splint tests (H₂, O₂), litmus tests (NH₃, Cl₂), and bubble-through tests (CO₂, SO₂).

Quick-Fire Rules

Rule 1: A–Z dissolves in excess NaOH
Al³⁺ and Zn²⁺ — white ppt first, then dissolves in excess NaOH to give a colourless solution.
Rule 2: Only Zn²⁺ dissolves in BOTH
Zn²⁺ dissolves in excess NaOH AND excess NH₃. Use this to distinguish Zn²⁺ from Al³⁺.
Rule 3: Cu²⁺ = Dark Blue in NH₃
Light blue ppt first, then a dark blue solution in excess NH₃ — it's Cu²⁺. 100% guaranteed.
Rule 4: Strong vs weak alkali
NaOH ionises completely: NaOH(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq). NH₃ ionises partially: NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq).
Rule 5: Acidify before Ag⁺ or Ba²⁺
Anion tests involve acidification — add dilute nitric acid first so CO₃²⁻ and OH⁻ don't give false positive white precipitates.
Rule 6: Two tests give NH₃ gas
NH₄⁺ + NaOH (warm) AND NO₃⁻ + NaOH + Al foil (warm) both evolve ammonia gas that turns moist red litmus paper blue.

Cation Tests — Colour Coded

What's happening: Tests for cations involve alkalis (aqueous sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia), which ionise in water to produce hydroxide (OH⁻) ions. The hydroxide ions react with most metal cations to produce metal hydroxides.
Complete ionisation of NaOH in water:
NaOH(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
Partial ionisation of NH₃ in water:
NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
Identify cations based on: ① Formation of a precipitate (if any) when a few drops of alkali are added → ② Colour of the precipitate formed (if any) → ③ Solubility of the precipitate (if any) in excess alkali
Cation Add aqueous sodium hydroxide dropwise till in excess Add aqueous ammonia dropwise till in excess
Ammonium (NH₄⁺) No precipitate is produced. Colourless and pungent ammonia gas that turns moist red litmus paper blue is evolved when warmed. ✗ No precipitate is produced.
Calcium (Ca²⁺) White precipitate of Ca(OH)₂, that is insoluble in excess NaOH(aq). ✗ No precipitate is produced.
Aluminium (Al³⁺) ★ A–Z White precipitate of Al(OH)₃ is produced, which dissolves in excess NaOH(aq) to form a colourless solution. White precipitate of Al(OH)₃, that is insoluble in excess NH₃(aq).
Zinc (Zn²⁺) ★ A–Z White precipitate of Zn(OH)₂ is produced, which dissolves in excess NaOH(aq) to form a colourless solution. White precipitate of Zn(OH)₂ is produced, which dissolves in excess NH₃(aq) to form a colourless solution.
Iron(II) (Fe²⁺) Green precipitate of Fe(OH)₂, that is insoluble in excess NaOH(aq). Green precipitate of Fe(OH)₂, that is insoluble in excess NH₃(aq).
Iron(III) (Fe³⁺) Red-brown precipitate of Fe(OH)₃, that is insoluble in excess NaOH(aq). Red-brown precipitate of Fe(OH)₃, that is insoluble in excess NH₃(aq).
Copper(II) (Cu²⁺) Light blue precipitate of Cu(OH)₂, that is insoluble in excess NaOH(aq). Light blue precipitate of Cu(OH)₂ is produced, which dissolves in excess NH₃(aq) to form a DARK BLUE solution.

Anion Tests

The approach: Tests for anions involve acidification, followed by evolution of gas or precipitation. Adding dilute nitric acid first removes CO₃²⁻ and OH⁻ that would give false positive white precipitates.
AnionTestObservation
Carbonate (CO₃²⁻) Add dilute acid. Bubble gas through limewater (aqueous calcium hydroxide). Effervescence of a colourless and odourless gas is observed. White precipitate of CaCO₃ is produced when gas is bubbled through limewater.
Chloride (Cl⁻) Add dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate. White precipitate of AgCl is produced.
Iodide (I⁻) Add dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate. Yellow precipitate of AgI is produced.
Sulfate (SO₄²⁻) Add dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous barium nitrate. White precipitate of BaSO₄ is produced.
Nitrate (NO₃⁻) Add aqueous sodium hydroxide and a small piece of aluminium foil. Warm the mixture. Colourless and pungent ammonia gas that turns moist red litmus paper blue is evolved when warmed.

Distinguishing Cl⁻ vs I⁻

Cl⁻ — Chloride
Dilute HNO₃ + AgNO₃(aq) → White ppt (AgCl)
I⁻ — Iodide
Dilute HNO₃ + AgNO₃(aq) → Yellow ppt (AgI)
Same reagent, different colour: Cl⁻ and I⁻ use the exact same test (dilute nitric acid, then aqueous silver nitrate). Only the precipitate colour tells them apart — white for chloride, yellow for iodide.

Gas Tests

GasTestObservation
Hydrogen (H₂) Place a lighted splint at the mouth of the test tube. Colourless and odourless gas extinguishes the lighted splint with a "pop" sound
Oxygen (O₂) Insert a glowing splint into the test tube. Colourless and odourless gas relights the glowing splint
Carbon dioxide (CO₂) Bubble the gas through limewater (aqueous calcium hydroxide). Colourless and odourless gas produces a white precipitate of CaCO₃
Ammonia (NH₃) Place a piece of moist red litmus paper at the mouth of the test tube. Colourless and pungent gas turns moist red litmus paper BLUE
Chlorine (Cl₂) Place a piece of moist blue litmus paper at the mouth of the test tube. Yellow-green and pungent gas turns moist blue litmus paper red and eventually bleaches it
Sulfur dioxide (SO₂) Bubble the gas through aqueous acidified potassium manganate(VII). Colourless and pungent gas turns aqueous acidified KMnO₄ from purple to colourless
Gas Memory Groups:
Splint tests: H₂ (lighted splint, POP) | O₂ (glowing splint relights)
Litmus tests: NH₃ (moist red → blue) | Cl₂ (moist blue → red, then bleached)
Bubble-through tests: CO₂ (limewater → white ppt) | SO₂ (acidified KMnO₄ → colourless)

Easy Confusions

NH₃ vs Cl₂
Both are pungent! NH₃ is colourless and turns moist RED litmus blue. Cl₂ is yellow-green and turns moist BLUE litmus red, then bleaches it.
H₂ vs O₂
Both are colourless and odourless! H₂ uses a LIGHTED splint (pop sound). O₂ uses a GLOWING splint (relights).
CO₂ vs SO₂
Both bubble-through tests! CO₂ is odourless (limewater → white ppt). SO₂ is pungent (KMnO₄ purple → colourless).

QA Strategy — Systematic Approach

What is QA? Qualitative analysis is a method used to identify elements and/or compounds present in an unknown substance, using physical tests (based on pH, smell, colour and solubility) and chemical tests (identification of cations, anions and gases).
Step 1 — Physical ObservationLook at the colour of the solid and the solution. Coloured solutions → transition metal (Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺, Cu²⁺). White solid, colourless solution → Ca²⁺, Al³⁺, Zn²⁺, NH₄⁺
↓
Step 2 — Add NaOH dropwise, then in excess
Green ppt → Fe²⁺ Red-brown ppt → Fe³⁺ Light blue ppt → Cu²⁺ White ppt → Ca²⁺, Al³⁺ or Zn²⁺ No ppt, gas on warming → NH₄⁺
For white ppt: does it dissolve in excess NaOH? → A–Z (Al³⁺, Zn²⁺). Insoluble → Ca²⁺
↓
Step 3 — Add NH₃ dropwise, then in excess (to confirm)
Light blue ppt, dark blue solution in excess → Cu²⁺ ✓ White ppt dissolves in excess → Zn²⁺ (Al³⁺ stays insoluble) No ppt at all → Ca²⁺
↓
Step 4 — Test for AnionsAcidify with dilute nitric acid first! Then aqueous barium nitrate (for SO₄²⁻), aqueous silver nitrate (for Cl⁻ / I⁻), dilute acid alone + limewater (for CO₃²⁻), NaOH + Al foil + warm (for NO₃⁻)
↓
Step 5 — Test any evolved gasesMatch gas colour + smell + specific test → identify H₂, O₂, CO₂, NH₃, Cl₂ or SO₂

Distinguishing Similar Ions

Pair to DistinguishKey TestResult
Al³⁺ vs Zn²⁺Add excess NH₃Only Zn²⁺ dissolves in excess NH₃ to form a colourless solution. Al³⁺ remains as a white ppt.
Ca²⁺ vs Al³⁺ / Zn²⁺Add NH₃Ca²⁺ gives NO precipitate with NH₃ at all. Al³⁺ and Zn²⁺ give white ppt.
Fe²⁺ vs Fe³⁺Colour of ppt with NaOH / NH₃Fe²⁺ = green ppt. Fe³⁺ = red-brown ppt. Both insoluble in excess.
NH₄⁺ vs other cationsAdd NaOH + warmNH₄⁺ gives NO ppt, but colourless pungent gas (NH₃) that turns moist red litmus paper blue.
Cl⁻ vs I⁻Dilute HNO₃ + AgNO₃(aq)Cl⁻ = white ppt (AgCl). I⁻ = yellow ppt (AgI).
SO₄²⁻ vs CO₃²⁻Add dilute acidCO₃²⁻ gives effervescence of CO₂ (white ppt with limewater). SO₄²⁻ does not react with dilute acid.

Solubility Rules — One Column Per Rule

SPAN
The Always-Soluble Squad
S — Sodium (Na⁺)
P — Potassium (K⁺)
A — Ammonium (NH₄⁺)
N — Nitrates (NO₃⁻)
✓ ALL their salts are soluble. Zero exceptions. This is why nitrates and sodium salts are used in precipitation reactions.
Chlorides (Cl⁻)
✓ Soluble, except…
"Pure Art Courses"
Pure — Pb²⁺ (PbCl₂)
Art — Ag⁺ (AgCl)
Courses — Chlorides
Br⁻ and I⁻ follow the same pattern (AgBr cream, AgI yellow). PbCl₂ is insoluble in COLD water but dissolves in HOT.
Sulfates (SO₄²⁻)
✓ Soluble, except…
"Sciences"
Biology — Ba²⁺ (BaSO₄)
Chemistry — Ca²⁺ (CaSO₄)
Physics — Pb²⁺ (PbSO₄)
This is why BaSO₄ (white ppt, insoluble in acid) is the SO₄²⁻ test, and why lead won't react with H₂SO₄ (PbSO₄ coating).
Carbonates (CO₃²⁻)
✗ Insoluble, except…
The SPA crew:
Na⁺ (sodium)
K⁺ (potassium)
NH₄⁺ (ammonium)
Insoluble carbonates (CaCO₃, ZnCO₃, CuCO₃…) are perfect excess reactants for the filtration salt-prep method.
Hydroxides (OH⁻)
✗ Insoluble, except…
Na⁺ (NaOH)
K⁺ (KOH)
Ba²⁺ (Ba(OH)₂)
NH₄⁺ is NOT here — Ba²⁺ takes its spot!
Insoluble hydroxides are exactly the precipitates you see in QA cation tests (Fe(OH)₂ green, Fe(OH)₃ red-brown, Cu(OH)₂ light blue…).
Phosphates (PO₄³⁻)
✗ Insoluble, except…
The SPA crew again:
Na⁺ (sodium)
K⁺ (potassium)
NH₄⁺ (ammonium)
Same exceptions as carbonates — if you know one, you know both.
The whole system in one breath: SPAN salts are always soluble. Chlorides are soluble except "Pure Art Courses" (Pb, Ag). Sulfates are soluble except the "Sciences" (Ba, Ca, Pb). Carbonates, hydroxides and phosphates flip to insoluble — except Na⁺, K⁺, NH₄⁺ (with Ba²⁺ replacing NH₄⁺ for hydroxides).

Laboratory Methods of Preparing Salts

The big idea: The method of salt preparation depends on the salt's solubility in water. Ask two questions in order: ① Is the salt soluble? ② Are the starting materials soluble?
Q1 — Is the salt to be prepared soluble in water?
NO → Insoluble salt → Method (A) Precipitation YES → Soluble salt → go to Q2
↓
Q2 — Are the starting materials for making the salt soluble in water?
NO (Non-SPA salts) → Method (B) Filtration — acid + excess insoluble reactant YES (SPA salts — Group 1 or ammonium cations) → Method (C) Titration

Method (A) — Precipitation (Insoluble Salts)

A precipitate is an insoluble chemical produced during a chemical reaction. ALL insoluble salts can be prepared by the precipitation method. Mix a soluble salt (e.g. a nitrate) containing the cation with a soluble salt (e.g. a sodium salt) containing the anion.

Steps: Add one aqueous solution to the other aqueous solution → Stir thoroughly until no more precipitate forms → Filter and collect the residue (which contains the precipitate); discard the filtrate → Wash the residue with deionised water to remove unwanted reactants → Dry the residue between sheets of filter paper.

Method (B) — Filtration (Soluble Salts NOT containing Group 1 / Ammonium)

React warm dilute acid with an excess insoluble reactant: a moderately reactive metal, an insoluble base, or an insoluble carbonate. Warm only when using a metal or insoluble base — carbonates react quickly, so no heating is needed.

Steps: Add excess reactant to warm dilute acid, stir until no more reacts → Filter the mixture to obtain the filtrate → Heat the filtrate till the point of saturation ( CANNOT evaporate to dryness — crystals will decompose upon heating) → Test for saturation by dipping a glass rod into the solution (optional) → Cool the filtrate to allow crystals to form → Filter to obtain the crystals as residue → Wash with a small amount of COLD deionised water → Dry crystals between pieces of filter paper.

Why excess? To ensure ALL the acid is completely used up — the leftover insoluble reactant is easily removed by filtration.

CombinationExamples of reactants
Acid + metalMg, Al, Zn, Fe (moderately reactive metals only)
Acid + insoluble baseMgO, ZnO, CuO, Fe(OH)₃, Cu(OH)₂
Acid + insoluble carbonateMgCO₃, ZnCO₃, CuCO₃
Acids usedHCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄
✗ The acid + metal method is NOT suitable for:
• Unreactive metals — lead and copper do not react with dilute acids
• Very reactive metals — sodium, potassium and calcium react too vigorously (explosive!)
• Making salts that are insoluble in water — e.g. PbCl₂, PbSO₄, AgCl (use precipitation instead)
✗ The PbCl₂ trap: Can we make PbCl₂ via PbO(s) + 2HCl(aq) → PbCl₂(s) + H₂O(l)? NO! If the product starts off as a solid, it will not fully react to completion — the insoluble PbCl₂ layer coats the PbO and stops the reaction. Insoluble salts like PbCl₂ must be made by precipitation.

Method (C) — Titration (Group 1 or Ammonium Salts)

Soluble salts containing Group 1 or ammonium cations are prepared by reacting an acid with an alkali (or a carbonate solution). Both starting materials are soluble, so nothing can be filtered off — a titration must first find the exact volume of acid that neutralises a known volume of alkali. Sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are prepared using the titration method.

Part 1 (with indicator): Fill a burette with the dilute acid; note the initial reading (V₁ cm³) → Pipette 25.0 cm³ of aqueous alkali into a conical flask → Add 2 to 3 drops of an indicator (e.g. phenolphthalein or methyl orange) → Add the acid slowly from the burette until the endpoint, where ONE drop of acid causes the indicator to change colour permanently → Record the final reading (V₂ cm³). Volume of acid needed for complete neutralisation = (V₂ − V₁) cm³.

Part 2 (without indicator): Repeat the titration WITHOUT the indicator — the indicator would make the salt impure — by adding the same volume (V₂ − V₁) cm³ of acid → Transfer to a crucible and heat to evaporate the water to form a saturated solution (glass rod test: crystals form on the cool rod = saturated) → Cool the hot saturated solution so the salt can crystallise → Filter to obtain the crystals and rinse with a little cold deionised water → Dry by pressing between sheets of filter paper.

Worked Examples from the Handout

(a) Acid + Metal — Zinc sulfate

Zn(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + H₂(g)

Dissolve (excess zinc, constant stirring) → Filter (remove unreacted zinc) → Concentrate (evaporate to about one-third the original volume) → Crystallise (cool to room temperature) → Filter, wash, dry.

(b) Acid + Insoluble Base — Copper(II) sulfate

CuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l)

Add CuO to sulfuric acid until no more can dissolve → filter to remove excess CuO (residue) → concentrate, crystallise, filter the filtrate → copper(II) sulfate crystals.

(c) Acid + Carbonate — Calcium nitrate

CaCO₃(s) + 2HNO₃(aq) → Ca(NO₃)₂(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)

Carbonates react quickly with acids, so no heating is needed. Add calcium carbonate until no more dissolves → filter → concentrate, crystallise, filter.

Types of Oxides

The quick sort: Metal + oxygen → usually a basic oxide. Non-metal + oxygen → usually an acidic oxide. Then learn the two exception clubs: the amphoteric trio (metal oxides that swing both ways) and the neutral trio (non-metal oxides that react with nothing).
ACIDIC Oxides
Oxides of NON-METALS
Reacts with: bases / alkalis → salt + water
In water: many dissolve to form acids
Examples: CO₂ (→ carbonic acid), SO₂ (→ sulfurous acid), SO₃ (→ sulfuric acid), NO₂
SiO₂ is acidic but insoluble in water
Links to QA: CO₂ and SO₂ are your acidic gases — they turn damp blue litmus red.
BASIC Oxides
Oxides of METALS
Reacts with: acids → salt + water
In water: a few dissolve to form alkalis (Na₂O, K₂O, CaO)
Examples: Na₂O, K₂O, CaO, MgO, CuO, Fe₂O₃
Most (MgO, CuO, Fe₂O₃) are insoluble — perfect excess reactants for salt prep!
e.g. CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O — the filtration method classic.
AMPHOTERIC Oxides
Metal oxides that react BOTH ways
Reacts with: BOTH acids AND bases → salt + water
The most common three:
Al₂O₃ — aluminium oxide
ZnO — zinc oxide
PbO — lead(II) oxide
e.g. ZnO + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂O
and ZnO + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + H₂O
Same A–Z–P trio as the amphoteric hydroxides in QA — Al and Zn are exactly why those white ppts dissolve in excess NaOH!
NEUTRAL Oxides
Non-metal oxides that react with NOTHING
Reacts with: neither acids nor bases
Effect on litmus: none — neutral to indicators
The most common three:
CO — carbon monoxide
NO — nitrogen monoxide
H₂O — water
Trap: CO is neutral but CO₂ is acidic; NO is neutral but NO₂ is acidic. One extra oxygen flips the type!

Classifying an Oxide — Decision Path

Q1 — Is it a metal oxide or non-metal oxide?
METAL → basic… unless it's Al₂O₃ / ZnO / PbO → amphoteric NON-METAL → acidic… unless it's CO / NO / H₂O → neutral
↓
Q2 — Confirm by reaction
Reacts with acid only → BASIC Reacts with alkali only → ACIDIC Reacts with BOTH → AMPHOTERIC Reacts with NEITHER → NEUTRAL
Memory hooks: Amphoteric = "A Zany Plumber" (Al₂O₃, ZnO, PbO). Neutral = "CO NO H₂O" — say it out loud, it almost rhymes ("see-oh, en-oh, aitch-two-oh"). Everything else follows the metal/non-metal rule.

Chemical Bonding & Structure

The big idea: Chemical bonding occurs in both elements and compounds. Most atoms bond to achieve a stable (usually duplet or octet) electronic configuration with a completely filled valence electron shell, similar to noble gases. ALL types of chemical bonding involve electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged particles.

Types of Chemical Bonding and Structure

Property IONIC
Giant ionic lattice		 COVALENT
Simple molecular		 COVALENT
Giant covalent		 METALLIC
Giant metallic lattice
Description Electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions Electrostatic forces of attraction between the positively charged nuclei of atoms and their shared pair(s) of electrons Electrostatic forces of attraction between metal cations and sea of delocalised valence electrons
Formation Metal atoms transfer their valence electrons to non-metal atoms Two atoms share at least one pair of valence electrons Metal atoms lose valence electrons to form metal cations surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons that can move freely between the cations
Particles Oppositely charged ions in a regular lattice Simple (discrete) molecules Extensive network of atoms Lattice of metal cations + sea of delocalised valence electrons
Melting & boiling points High — large amount of thermal energy required to overcome the strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions Low — only a small amount of thermal energy required to overcome the weak intermolecular forces of attraction between molecules High — large amount of thermal energy required to break all the strong covalent bonds between atoms in the extensive network High (except Group 1 metals and mercury) — large amount of thermal energy required to overcome the strong electrostatic forces between metal cations and the sea of delocalised electrons
Conducts electricity? ✓ Yes in molten and aqueous states (free-moving ions act as mobile charge carriers) ✗ No in all physical states (except acids and alkalis, which ionise in water) ✗ No in all physical states (except graphite) ✓ Yes in solid and molten states (delocalised valence electrons act as mobile charge carriers)
Solubility Mostly soluble in water; insoluble in organic solvents Mostly insoluble in water; soluble in organic solvents Insoluble in water and organic solvents Insoluble in water and organic solvents
Others Hard and brittle NIL Hard (diamond, silicon dioxide); slippery (graphite) High thermal conductivity; high density (except Group 1 metals); malleable and ductile

Giant Covalent Substances — Diamond vs Graphite

Diamond

Hard — all the carbon atoms are held rigidly in fixed positions by strong covalent bonds, which cannot be broken easily.

Does NOT conduct electricity — each carbon atom forms covalent bonds with FOUR other carbon atoms. All the valence electrons are used for bonding, so there are no delocalised electrons to act as mobile charge carriers.

Graphite

Slippery — each layer of carbon atoms can slide over another layer easily due to the weak intermolecular forces of attraction between the layers.

CAN conduct electricity — each carbon atom only uses THREE out of four valence electrons for covalent bonding, leaving one delocalised valence electron per carbon atom. These move freely along the layers as mobile charge carriers.

Deducing the Bonding and Structure of a Substance

Start — Melting and boiling points?
LOW → Simple covalent substances OR some metals (Group 1 metals or mercury) HIGH → Giant lattice structures (metals / ionic compounds) OR giant covalent substances
↓
If LOW — Conducts electricity?
No, in all physical states → Simple covalent substance (check physical state at r.t.p.: solid e.g. sulfur, iodine · liquid e.g. water, bromine · gas e.g. oxygen, methane) Yes, in aqueous state only → Simple covalent substance (acidic or alkaline gas, e.g. hydrogen chloride, ammonia) Yes, in solid and molten states → Group 1 metal or mercury
↓
If HIGH — Conducts electricity in molten state?
No → Giant covalent substance (except graphite) Yes → Giant lattice structure → then ask: conducts in SOLID state? Yes → Metal. No → Ionic compound

Pure Metals vs Alloys

Pure Metals

Atoms are arranged regularly in layers. When a force is applied, the layers of metal atoms can slide over each other easily. Hence pure metals are malleable (can be bent or flattened into thin sheets) and ductile (can be pulled into wires without breaking).

Alloys

An alloy is a solid mixture of a metal and one or a few other elements. The constituent atoms have different sizes, which disrupt the regular arrangement of atoms. A larger force is required to make the layers slide over each other, so an alloy is stronger and harder than a pure metal.

Exam technique: The three bonding definitions all follow the same template — "electrostatic forces of attraction between ___ and ___". Ionic: oppositely charged ions. Covalent: positively charged nuclei + shared pair(s) of electrons. Metallic: metal cations + sea of delocalised valence electrons. Learn the template once, swap in the particles.

Reading the Ar values. Ar is the average mass of the atoms of an element compared with 1⁄12 the mass of one carbon-12 atom. It is a ratio, so it carries no units — never write “Ar = 35.5 g”. It is an average over the natural isotopes, which is why chlorine sits at 35.5 rather than 35 or 37.

Physics Mnemonics & Memory Tricks

Eleven tabs, three topics. Start here if your brain has gone blank — these are the hooks that pull the rest of the topic back.

The 5 kinematics symbols
s u v a t
s = displacement u = initial velocity v = final velocity a = acceleration t = time
Every equation of motion uses four of these five. Write down the three you know and the one you want — the equation that contains exactly those four is the one to use.
Picking the right equation
MISSING LETTER
no s → v = u + at no v → s = ut + ½at² no t → v² = u² + 2as no a → s = ½(u+v)t no u → s = vt − ½at² (derived)
Ask "which quantity do I neither know nor need?" — then use the equation that leaves that letter out. No trial and error needed. The no u one is not on the formula sheet — derive it from u = v − at if you want it.
Reading motion graphs
SLOPE DOWN, AREA UP
gradient: s → v → a area: a → v → s
Going down the chain (displacement → velocity → acceleration) you take the gradient. Going back up you take the area under the graph. Two rules cover every graph question.
Newton's three laws
LAZY · FORMULA · FIGHT BACK
1st = Lazy (inertia) 2nd = Formula (F = ma) 3rd = Fight back (pairs)
1st: objects are lazy, they keep doing what they were doing. 2nd: unbalanced force gives the formula FR = ma. 3rd: push something and it pushes back, equally and oppositely.
Is it a true action–reaction pair?
MOBS
M = same Magnitude O = Opposite direction B = different Bodies S = Same nature
All four must hold. The classic trap: weight and normal force on a TV are not a pair — they act on the same body and are different natures (one contact, one non-contact).
Terminal velocity in one line
DRAG = WEIGHT
resultant force = 0 N a = 0 m s⁻² v = constant
Air resistance grows as speed grows. The moment it equals the weight, the forces balance — constant velocity, not zero velocity. Marks are lost every year for saying "it stops accelerating and slows down".
The six energy stores
Kangaroos Grab Elastic Chocolate In Nests
Kinetic Gravitational Elastic Chemical Internal Nuclear
Energy is stored in these six. Heat, light, sound and electricity are not stores — they are energy in transit, i.e. transfer pathways.
The four transfer pathways
M · H · W · E
Mechanically (force × distance) Heating (temperature difference) Waves (EM + sound) Electrically (current)
Energy moves between stores by exactly one of these four routes. Name the route and the two stores and you have a full-mark energy answer.
When is work done?
NO MOVE → NO WORK
W = F × s s is measured along the force
Carrying a box horizontally does zero work against gravity — the weight acts downwards but the box moves sideways, so the distance moved in the direction of the force is 0 m.
Mass vs weight
MATTER vs GRAVITY
Mass = amount of matter, kg, scalar Weight = force of gravity, N, vector
Your mass is the same on the Moon; your weight is about six times smaller because g falls from 10 N kg⁻¹ to 1.6 N kg⁻¹.

Kinematics — The Five Quantities

The big idea: Kinematics describes how things move without asking why. Everything reduces to five quantities and a hard split between scalars (size only) and vectors (size and direction). Most lost marks in this topic come from swapping a vector for its scalar twin.

The quantity table

Quantity Definition SI unit Type Symbol
Distance The total length of path travelled by an object metre (m) Scalar d
Displacement The distance measured in a straight line from the starting point, in a stated direction metre (m) Vector s
Speed Distance travelled per unit time m s⁻¹ Scalar —
Velocity Displacement per unit time (i.e. rate of change of displacement) m s⁻¹ Vector u, v
Acceleration Rate of change of velocity — how fast the velocity changes each second m s⁻² Vector a
average speed = total distance ÷ total time  ·  average velocity = net displacement ÷ total time  ·  acceleration = (v − u) ÷ t

Distance vs displacement — the split that costs marks

Distance — scalar

Adds up everything you walked, no matter which way you turned. It can only ever increase. A full lap of a track gives a large distance.

Displacement — vector

Only cares where you ended up relative to where you started, plus a direction. It can decrease, and it can be zero. A full lap gives zero displacement.

Worked example — circular track Practice 1 Q1

An athlete runs half a lap of a circular track of radius 20 m, from A to the opposite point B, in 7.5 s.

(a) Average speed. Distance = half the circumference = 0.5 × π × (40 m) = 62.832 m.
Average speed = 62.832 m ÷ 7.5 s = 8.4 m s⁻¹ (2 s.f.)
(b) Magnitude of displacement A → B. The straight line from A to B is a diameter = 40 m.
(c) Why is average velocity zero over one complete lap? After one complete lap the athlete returns to his original position, so his net displacement is zero. Since velocity is displacement per unit time, a zero displacement gives a zero average velocity — even though his average speed is large.

Exam traps to watch

The trapWhat the examiner wants instead
Writing "velocity = distance / time" Velocity is displacement per unit time. Reserve "distance" for speed.
Giving a displacement with no direction State the direction: "200 m, south of point A". A vector answer without a direction is incomplete.
Assuming negative acceleration always means slowing down A negative sign only means "in the negative direction". An object speeding up in the negative direction also has negative acceleration.
Assuming constant speed means no acceleration Moving in a circle at constant speed still means the direction of velocity is changing, so the object is accelerating.
Rounding too early Keep full precision through the working; round only the final answer, and match the significant figures of the data (usually 2 or 3 s.f.).

Describing motion with diagrams

Motion Graphs

Two rules run this whole tab: the gradient of a graph gives you the quantity one step "down" the chain, and the area under a graph gives you the quantity one step "up". Everything else is shape recognition.
displacement–time graphgradient = velocity. Area under it means nothing.
↓ gradient     ↑ area
velocity–time graphgradient = acceleration  ·  area under = displacement
↓ gradient     ↑ area
acceleration–time grapharea under = change in velocity

Displacement–time graphs

ShapeWhat it meansHow to read it
Horizontal lineAt restGradient = 0, so velocity = 0. Position is not changing.
Straight sloping lineConstant velocityVelocity = gradient = Δs ÷ Δt. Steeper line = faster.
Curve getting steeperAcceleratingGradient increasing, so velocity increasing. A freely falling object gives this shape.
Curve flattening offDeceleratingGradient decreasing towards zero — the object is coming to rest.
Line sloping downwardsMoving back towards the startNegative gradient = negative velocity, i.e. motion in the opposite direction.

Velocity–time graphs

ShapeWhat it meansHow to read it
Horizontal line above the axisConstant velocityGradient = 0, so acceleration = 0 and the forces are balanced.
Straight sloping lineUniform accelerationa = gradient = (v − u) ÷ t. The equations of motion are valid here.
Curve flattening towards a horizontal lineApproaching terminal velocityAcceleration decreasing to zero as air resistance builds up to equal the weight.
Line crossing the time axisThe object reversed directionAbove axis and below axis are opposite directions. Areas on opposite sides cancel when finding displacement.
Area under the lineDisplacementSplit into triangles and rectangles: triangle = ½ × base × height, rectangle = base × height.
Sketching the skydiver Practice 2 Q2

A skydiver reaches a terminal velocity of 55.6 m s⁻¹ after 10.0 s, falls for 70.0 s, opens her parachute and quickly slows to a new terminal velocity of 10.2 m s⁻¹, then lands 105 s later.

Stage 1 — 0 to 10 s: a steep curve rising from the origin and flattening, because air resistance increases as speed increases, so acceleration decreases.
Stage 2 — 10 s to 80 s: a horizontal line at 55.6 m s⁻¹. Air resistance now equals weight, resultant force is 0 N.
Stage 3 — parachute opens: a steep drop that curves and levels out at 10.2 m s⁻¹ — the larger cross-sectional area gives much greater air resistance, so there is a large upward resultant force and a deceleration that shrinks to zero.
Stage 4: horizontal at 10.2 m s⁻¹ until she lands.
Why the equations of motion cannot be used here: the acceleration is not uniform for parts of the journey, and the kinematics equations are only valid for uniform acceleration.
Marks are awarded for the boring things. In a sketch question the three marks usually go to: (1) axes labelled with quantity and unit, (2) correct shape including curvature, (3) key values marked on both axes. Draw the shape first, then go back and label.

Comparing the two graph types

Reading area off a velocity–time graph

The skydiver, stage by stage

Equations of Motion

Health warning: these five equations are only valid when the acceleration is uniform (constant). If a question mentions terminal velocity, a parachute or "changing acceleration", the equations do not apply for that stage — use a graph instead.

The five equations

v = u + at
leaves out s
Use when you don't know and don't want the displacement.
s = ut + ½at²
leaves out v
Use when the final velocity is neither given nor asked for.
v² = u² + 2as
leaves out t
Use when time is not mentioned anywhere in the question.
s = ½(u + v)t
leaves out a
Use when acceleration is unknown but both velocities are given.
s = vt − ½at²
leaves out u
Use when the initial velocity is neither given nor wanted — typically a body already moving when the clock starts, or a question that only quotes the speed at the end.
The fifth one is derived, not given. It is not printed on the formula sheet, so show the two lines if you use it in an exam:

From v = u + at, rearrange to u = v − at.
Substitute into s = ut + ½at²:
s = (v − at)t + ½at² = vt − at² + ½at² = vt − ½at²

Watch the sign. The second term is minus ½at², not plus. Writing it as vt + ½at² by reflex from s = ut + ½at² is the single most common slip with this equation.

When it actually saves you time. Anything working backwards from a known final velocity: "a car is travelling at 25 m s⁻¹ when it starts braking at 4.0 m s⁻² — how far does it go in the next 3.0 s?" Here v, a and t are known and u is not wanted, so s = vt − ½at² gives the answer in one step. You can always reach the same answer with the other four, it just takes an extra line.

How to attack any EOM question

1. Choose a positive direction and write it down. "Taking downwards as positive" earns nothing on its own but prevents almost every sign error.
↓
2. List s, u, v, a, t. Write the three you know, put a "?" on the one you want, and cross out the fifth.
↓
3. Pick the equation missing the crossed-out letter. Substitute with units, then solve.
↓
4. Sanity-check the sign and size. A car should not decelerate at 400 m s⁻², and a dropped ball should not have negative downward velocity.

Free fall

SituationWhat to use
Released from restu = 0, a = g. With g = 10 m s⁻²: s = ½gt² and v = gt.
Thrown upwardsTake up as positive: a = −g throughout, including at the very top. At maximum height v = 0 but a is still −g.
Air resistance negligibleAll objects fall with the same acceleration regardless of mass — a heavier nail takes exactly the same time to fall as a lighter one.
Air resistance significantAcceleration decreases as speed increases; the object may reach terminal velocity. EOM no longer valid.
Worked example — block down a ramp Practice 2 Q1

A block is released from rest and slides down a frictionless ramp 5.0 m long, reaching the end 1.6 s later.

(a) Velocity at the end of the ramp. Known: s = 5.0 m, u = 0, t = 1.6 s. Wanted: v. Missing: a → use s = ½(u + v)t.
5.0 = 0.5 × v × 1.6 → v = 6.3 m s⁻¹ (2 s.f.)
(b) Acceleration. Known: s, u, t. Wanted: a. Missing: v → use s = ut + ½at².
5.0 = 0 + ½ × a × (1.6)² → a = 3.9 m s⁻² (2 s.f.)
(c) Average speed for the whole journey (5.0 m on the ramp in 1.6 s, then 5.0 m on a rough surface in 3.2 s):
average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 10.0 m ÷ 4.8 s = 2.1 m s⁻¹ (2 s.f.)
Worked example — the Mars descent Dynamics Practice Q2

A 250 kg probe fires reverse thrusters at 40 m s⁻¹ and lands 30 s later at 0.75 m s⁻¹. Take gMars = 4.0 N kg⁻¹, no air resistance.

Step 1 — acceleration. Taking downwards as positive: a = (v − u) ÷ t = (0.75 − 40) ÷ 30 = −1.31 m s⁻² (i.e. a deceleration).
Step 2 — resultant force. FR = ma = 250 × (−1.31) = −327 N, so there is a resultant force of 327 N upwards.
Step 3 — bring in the weight. Weight = mg = 250 × 4.0 = 1000 N downwards.
1000 − thrust = −327 → thrust ≈ 1.3 × 10³ N upwards.
Why this is a two-topic question: kinematics gives you a, then Newton's second law converts a into a force. Almost every Sec 3 dynamics problem has this shape.

Free fall — reading g off the graph

Forces, Mass & Weight

Definition to memorise: a force is a push or a pull on an object due to an interaction with another object. A force can make an object start moving, stop, speed up, slow down, or change direction — the "change in motion" phrase is what examiners look for.

The two families of force

Contact forces — objects must touch

Friction — opposes, or tends to oppose, motion between surfaces in contact.

Air resistance — the frictional force exerted by air that opposes the motion of a moving object.

Normal force — the push exerted by a surface on an object pressing on it, always perpendicular to the surface.

Tension — the pull exerted by a stretched spring, string or rope on an object attached to it.

Non-contact forces — act at a distance

Gravitational force — the pull exerted by the Earth's gravity on any object with mass. This is the object's weight.

Electrostatic force — attraction between unlike charges, repulsion between like charges.

Magnetic force — attraction between unlike poles, repulsion between like poles.

Mass vs weight

MassWeight
The amount of substance (matter) in the bodyThe force of gravity acting on the body
Constant in any locationDepends on the gravitational field strength at that location
Measured in kilograms (kg)Measured in newtons (N)
ScalarVector — it acts downwards, towards the centre of the Earth
Measured with a beam balance / electronic balanceMeasured with a spring balance (newton meter / force meter)

Gravitational field and field strength

W = mg  ·  weight (N) = mass (kg) × gravitational field strength (N kg⁻¹)
TermDefinition you should be able to write out
Gravitational fieldA region in which a mass experiences a force due to gravitational attraction.
Gravitational field strength, gThe gravitational force per unit mass placed at that point. Unit: N kg⁻¹.
On Earthg ≈ 10 N kg⁻¹ — a 1 kg mass experiences a gravitational force of 10 N.
On the Moong ≈ 1.6 N kg⁻¹ — the same 1 kg mass experiences only 1.6 N.
Numerically equal to…the acceleration of free fall for a body near the Earth, which is why 10 N kg⁻¹ and 10 m s⁻² are interchangeable.

Density carried over from LSS

density = mass ÷ volume  ·  SI unit kg m⁻³  ·  1.0 g cm⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³

Floats

An object placed in a liquid of higher density than its own will float.

Sinks

An object placed in a liquid of lower density than its own will sink.

Unit conversion, done slowly once: 1 g cm⁻³ = (1/1000 kg) ÷ (1/1 000 000 m³) = 1000 kg m⁻³. Multiply g cm⁻³ by 1000 to get kg m⁻³; divide to go back.

Newton's Laws & Free-Body Diagrams

Newton's first law

An object at rest will remain at rest, and an object in motion will continue to move at constant velocity, unless a resultant force acts on it.
If the forces are…Then the object…
Balanced (resultant force = 0 N)is in equilibrium: either at rest, or moving in a straight line at constant speed. Acceleration = 0 m s⁻².
Unbalanced (resultant force ≠ 0 N)accelerates in the direction of the resultant force — speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction.
The classic exam statement: "If the forces acting on an object are balanced, then the object must not be accelerating." It may well be moving — non-zero velocity does not mean non-zero resultant force. A 2 kg object gliding at 4 m s⁻¹ needs 0 N of resultant force to keep going.

Inertia — why the first law feels the way it does

IdeaExplanation
InertiaThe reluctance of a body to change its state of rest or motion. Newton's first law is also called the law of inertia.
Quantified by massThe greater the mass, the greater the inertia — a more massive object is harder to start, speed up, slow down or turn.
Seat beltsIn a collision a passenger in motion continues to move forward because of inertia. The seat belt exerts an external force on the passenger, decelerating them safely.
Box on an accelerating lorryThe box tends to stay where it was, so relative to the lorry it slides towards the back. When the lorry brakes, the box slides towards the front.
Passenger on a trainAs the train accelerates forwards, a frictionless passenger stays at rest relative to the ground, so she appears to move backwards relative to the train.

Newton's second law

The resultant force acting on an object is equal to the product of its mass and its acceleration, and the object accelerates in the direction of the resultant force.
FR = ma  ·  FR = resultant force (N), m = mass (kg), a = acceleration (m s⁻²)
1 N is the force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻², so 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².

Finding the resultant force

CaseMethod
Parallel forcesSimple addition (same direction) or subtraction (opposite directions). Choose a positive direction first.
Perpendicular forcesPythagoras for the magnitude, trigonometry for the direction. 3 N east + 4 N north gives 5 N at 37° east of north.
Non-parallel forcesDraw to scale using the tip-to-tail method or the parallelogram method, then measure — or calculate with trigonometry.
Static point mass, 3 forcesThe forces are balanced, so the three vectors form a closed vector triangle — the three arrows follow each other head to tail in a closed loop. (Preferred method.)

Free-body diagrams

What it isA diagram showing the object (as a dot, a block or a sketch) and only the forces acting on it.
Rule 1 — forces ON the object onlyForces the object exerts on its surroundings must not appear. Half of all lost marks live here.
Rule 2 — label every arrow fullyUse "type of force on object by source", e.g. "normal contact force on box by table".
Rule 3 — start the arrow from the right placeWeight acts from the centre of gravity; normal force acts from the contact surface.
Rule 4 — arrow length shows magnitudeIf the object is in equilibrium, opposing arrows must be drawn the same length.

Newton's third law

If body A exerts a force on body B, then body B exerts an equal and opposite force on body A. Forces always occur in action–reaction pairs.
All four must be trueCheck
Equal in magnitudeSame size, always — even when a lorry hits a mosquito.
Opposite in directionExactly antiparallel.
Acting on different bodiesThis is the one that catches people out. One force on A, one force on B.
Of the same natureBoth contact, or both gravitational — never one of each.
The naming convention that guarantees the mark: write "<type of force> by <object exerting> on <object experiencing>". Then the partner force is the same sentence with the two objects swapped. Swimming: "contact force by the wall on the boy" pairs with "contact force by the boy on the wall".
The TV on the table — the trap everyone falls into

A TV rests on a table. Four forces are in play: the gravitational force on the TV by the Earth (FET), the gravitational force on the Earth by the TV (FTE), the normal force on the TV by the table (n), and the normal force on the table by the TV (n′).

Genuine pairs: FET with FTE (both gravitational, different bodies) and n with n′ (both contact, different bodies).
NOT a pair: the weight of the TV and the normal force on the TV. They act on the same body and are of different natures (one non-contact, one contact). They happen to be equal here only because the TV is in equilibrium.
Why doesn't the Earth move towards a falling ball? The force on the Earth by the ball equals the force on the ball by the Earth, but since a = F/m and the Earth's mass is enormous, the Earth's acceleration is negligible.

Friction & Terminal Velocity

Definition: friction is the force that opposes, or tends to oppose, relative motion between two surfaces in contact. The "tends to" matters — friction acts on a stationary box you are pushing but failing to move.

Friction is not the enemy

Useful effectsUnwanted effects
Friction between shoes and the ground lets you walk without slipping; between tyres and road it lets cars accelerate, turn and brake. Surfaces heat up, causing wear and tear on moving parts.
Friction lets a belt drive a pulley, a nail hold in wood, and a car park on a slope without sliding. In machinery friction reduces efficiency, because a large amount of energy is transferred away as unwanted internal energy.

Ways to reduce friction

Ball and roller bearings between moving parts · surfaces separated by a lubricant · surfaces separated by an air cushion · smoother, streamlined shapes.

What friction depends on

The materials in contact · the roughness of the surfaces · it is proportional to the force pressing the surfaces together · and it is independent of the area of contact.

Terminal velocity — the four-stage story

Stage 1 — just releasedAir resistance is zero, so the only force is the weight. The resultant force is at its maximum and the object accelerates at g.
↓
Stage 2 — speeding upAs speed increases, air resistance increases. The resultant force (weight − air resistance) shrinks, so the acceleration decreases — the object is still speeding up, just less quickly.
↓
Stage 3 — terminal velocity reachedAir resistance has grown until it equals the weight. Resultant force = 0 N, acceleration = 0 m s⁻², and the object falls at a constant velocity.
↓
Stage 4 — parachute opensCross-sectional area jumps, so air resistance jumps above the weight. Now there is a resultant force upwards: the object decelerates until air resistance falls back to equal the weight, giving a new, lower terminal velocity.

What changes the size of the terminal velocity

FactorEffect and reason
Mass of the falling object A heavier object generally has a greater terminal velocity. Its weight is larger, so it must accelerate to a higher speed before air resistance can grow large enough to balance that weight.
Cross-sectional area A larger area (an open parachute, a spread-eagled skydiver) experiences greater air resistance at any given speed, so the balance point comes sooner — a lower terminal velocity.
Model answer for "explain what is meant by terminal velocity" [1]: it is the constant velocity of a falling object reached when the air resistance on the object is equal to the gravitational force (weight) on it. Say "constant velocity", not "maximum speed", and always name both forces.

Work, Energy & Power

The model: energy sits in stores and moves between them along pathways. It is never created or destroyed. The SI unit for energy and for work is the joule (J), and both are scalars.

The six energy stores

StoreAlso calledExample
Kinetickinetic energyAny object in motion with speed v
Gravitational potentialgravitational potential energyAn object raised above the ground
Elastic potentialelastic potential energyA stretched rubber band, a compressed spring
Chemical potentialchemical potential energyFood, fossil fuels, batteries
Internalinternal energyA hot object — the KE and PE of all its molecules
Nuclearnuclear energyThe nuclei of atoms; released by fission
Vocabulary that loses marks: heat, light, sound and electricity are not stores — they are energy in transit. Avoid "heat energy", "sound energy", "light energy" and "electrical energy". Say internal energy (or just "heat" as a transfer), and energy transferred by sound waves / electrically. Also do not mix the two models: stores are transferred, forms are converted.

The two formulas you must recall

EK = ½mv²
kinetic store
m in kg, v in m s⁻¹. Only the speed is squared — a very common slip.
EP = mgh
gravitational potential store
h is the height relative to the chosen reference level, usually the ground.

The four transfer pathways

PathwayExample
Mechanically, by a force acting over a distanceA force pushes a cart over a distance s, transferring energy to the cart's kinetic store.
By heating, due to a temperature differenceA hot pan transfers energy to the internal store of the butter, which melts.
By propagation of waves (electromagnetic and mechanical)Infrared from the Sun warms skin; sound waves from cymbals set eardrums vibrating.
Electrically, by an electric currentA dry cell transfers energy from its chemical potential store to the internal store of a bulb filament.

Principle of conservation of energy

(i) Energy cannot be created or destroyed. (ii) It can only be transferred from one store to another. (iii) The total energy of an isolated system is constant. (An isolated system is one that exchanges neither matter nor energy with its surroundings.)
Worked example — parcel down a smooth ramp

A 4.0 kg parcel slides down a smooth curved ramp from a height of 5.0 m. Take g = 10 m s⁻². Find the speed at the bottom.

By the principle of conservation of energy: loss in gravitational potential store = gain in kinetic store.
mgh = ½mv² → since the mass appears on both sides, it cancels: (10)(5.0) = ½v²
v = 10 m s⁻¹ — and notice the answer is independent of mass, which is why this is a favourite exam question.

Work done

W = F × s  ·  work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force  ·  unit: joule (J)
SituationWork done by that force
Lifting a 50 N box through 1.1 mPositive: W = 50 × 1.1 = 55 J
Carrying the same box 2.0 m horizontally at constant speedZero: the weight acts downwards but there is no vertical displacement, so W = 50 × 0 = 0 J
Your hand stopping a ball you catchNegative: the force on the ball is opposite to the ball's displacement, so the hand removes energy from the ball's kinetic store.

Work–energy theorem

FR × s = ½mv² − ½mu²  ·  the work done by the resultant force equals the change in the kinetic store.

Power

P = W ÷ t
work done per unit time
Power is the work done, or energy transferred, per unit time. Unit: J s⁻¹ = watt (W). Scalar.
P = F × v
force × velocity
A powerful machine is both strong (big force) and fast (big velocity). Handy for engines and jets.

Efficiency

efficiency = (useful energy output ÷ total energy input) × 100%
where total energy input = useful energy output + non-useful (wasted) energy
Worked example — the electric motor

An electric motor lifts a 10 N load through 5.0 m using 65 J of electrical input.

Useful output = work done on the load = 10 N × 5.0 m = 50 J.
Energy wasted = 65 − 50 = 15 J.
Efficiency = (50 ÷ 65) × 100% = 77%.
Efficiency is never 100% because some energy is always transferred to the internal store of the surroundings through friction and resistance.

Energy Resources & Singapore's Trilemma

Singapore's energy trilemma: as a small country with limited natural energy resources, Singapore has to balance energy security (supply that will not be disrupted), competitive pricing (affordable electricity), and environmental sustainability (renewable, low-impact resources). Almost every exam discussion question wants two of these three in tension.

Non-renewable — cannot be replenished, will run out

ResourceHow it worksAdvantagesDisadvantages
Fossil fuels Have energy in the chemical potential store; burning transfers energy by heating to water, producing steam that drives turbines. More reliable than weather-dependent resources; relatively cheap to produce. Gases produced during burning cause environmental pollution and contribute to global warming.
Nuclear fuels Uranium nuclei undergo fission, splitting into parts; energy moves from the nuclear store to the kinetic stores of those parts, heating water into steam. Low-carbon, reducing greenhouse gas emissions; high reliability and uninterrupted supply. Risk of accidents; pollution from improper disposal of radioactive waste.

Renewable — can be replenished

ResourceHow it worksAdvantagesDisadvantages
Biofuels Ethanol, biodiesel and biogas derived from biomass; energy sits in the chemical potential store and is released by burning. Widely available on a large scale; relatively cheap. Burning still produces gases that contribute to global warming.
Wind Energy in the kinetic store of the wind is transferred mechanically to the kinetic store of the turbine blades, which drive generators. Renewable; clean — no harmful gases produced. Intermittent — needs steady winds of about 20–25 km h⁻¹; noise pollution and loss of habitat.
Tides Changing high and low tides rotate turbines below the water surface; kinetic store of water → kinetic store of turbines. More reliable than wind or sun; clean. High cost of building tidal barrages; marine life affected by altered currents and noise.
Hydropower Water held behind a dam has energy in the gravitational potential store; releasing it transfers energy mechanically to the kinetic store of the water, spinning turbines. Renewable and continually regenerated; clean. High cost of dams; damming a river damages the surrounding environment.
Geothermal Water reaching volcanic hotspots is heated under pressure, gaining energy in its internal store, and is forced up as steam to drive turbines. Renewable; clean, naturally available energy. Release of poisonous gases such as hydrogen sulfide during drilling; only available in certain regions.
Solar Energy in the Sun's nuclear store travels as electromagnetic waves to solar panels made of semiconductors such as silicon, generating electricity. Clean method of producing electricity; well suited to Singapore's high year-round irradiance. Unavailable at night and weather-dependent; panels take up a lot of space.
Why not hydropower in Singapore? The height difference of the water source is the biggest contributor to the energy input of a hydroelectric plant, and Singapore has no large body of moving water with a drop of anything like 180 m. Solar is the sensible alternative: high average sunlight per unit area and plenty of flat, unobstructed rooftops.

Which Equation?

Most lost marks in Physics are not algebra mistakes. They are picking the wrong equation, then grinding through four correct lines to a wrong answer. This page is the chooser: every equation on the syllabus, what it needs, what it hands back, and one worked example behind a dropdown so you can see what the words actually mean.

The three-column habit. Before writing a single equation, split the question into three lists:

1. GIVEN — every number in the question, with its symbol and unit.
2. ASKED — the one quantity they want.
3. NEITHER — everything else.

Now pick the equation that contains your GIVEN and your ASKED, and nothing from the NEITHER list. If an equation drags in a quantity you neither have nor want, it is the wrong equation, no matter how familiar it looks.

Kinematics — the five equations of motion

Before you use any of these five, check one thing: is the acceleration uniform (constant)? If the v–t graph is a curve, or the question says the acceleration changes, all five are illegal — go to the graph methods below instead.
v = u + at
You need: any three of u, v, a, t
It gives you: the fourth one
Reach for it when: displacement s is neither given nor wanted
Trap: this is the only one of the five where s never appears — if the question mentions a distance, you probably want a different equation.
Show an exampleHide the example

A car accelerates uniformly from rest at 2.0 m s⁻² for 6.0 s. Find its final velocity.

GIVEN u = 0, a = 2.0, t = 6.0. ASKED v. NEITHER s — no distance anywhere.

v = u + at = 0 + (2.0)(6.0)

v = 12 m s⁻¹

s = ut + ½at²
You need: u, a, t
It gives you: displacement s
Reach for it when: you know how long the motion lasted and want the distance covered
Note: final velocity v is neither given nor wanted
Trap: ½at² means ½ × a × t², not (½at)². Square the time first, then multiply.
Show an exampleHide the example

A ball is thrown vertically upward at 20 m s⁻¹. Take g = 10 m s⁻² downward. How far above the hand is it after 1.5 s?

Take upward as positive, so u = +20 and a = −10.

s = ut + ½at² = (20)(1.5) + ½(−10)(1.5)² = 30 − 11.25

s = 18.75 ≈ 19 m above the hand. Note it is still rising: the sign convention did the work for you.

v² = u² + 2as
You need: any three of u, v, a, s
It gives you: the fourth one
Reach for it when: time t is neither given nor wanted
Note: braking distances, stopping distances, “how fast at the bottom” — anything where no clock is mentioned
Trap: you must take the square root at the end if you are solving for v or u. Forgetting it is the classic slip.
Show an exampleHide the example

A cyclist speeds up uniformly from 4.0 m s⁻¹ to 10.0 m s⁻¹ over 42 m of road. Find the acceleration.

GIVEN u = 4.0, v = 10.0, s = 42. ASKED a. NEITHER t — not mentioned once.

10.0² = 4.0² + 2a(42) → 100 = 16 + 84a → 84a = 84

a = 1.0 m s⁻²

s = ½(u + v)t
You need: u, v, t
It gives you: displacement s
Reach for it when: acceleration a is neither given nor wanted
Note: both velocities are quoted and you just want the distance
Trap: ½(u + v) is the average velocity, and averaging like this is only legal because the acceleration is uniform.
Show an exampleHide the example

A train slows uniformly from 30 m s⁻¹ to 10 m s⁻¹ over 40 s. How far does it travel?

GIVEN u = 30, v = 10, t = 40. ASKED s. NEITHER a — you are never asked for it.

s = ½(30 + 10)(40) = ½(40)(40)

s = 800 m

s = vt − ½at² (derived)
You need: v, a, t
It gives you: displacement s
Reach for it when: initial velocity u is neither given nor wanted
Note: the body is already moving when the clock starts and only the final speed is quoted
Trap: the sign is minus ½at². Copying the plus from s = ut + ½at² is the usual error. This one is not on the formula sheet, so derive it from u = v − at if you use it.
Show an exampleHide the example

A car is doing 25 m s⁻¹ the instant it stops braking at 4.0 m s⁻². How far did it travel in the final 3.0 s?

GIVEN v = 25, a = −4.0, t = 3.0. ASKED s. NEITHER u — the speed at the start of that 3 s is never mentioned.

s = vt − ½at² = (25)(3.0) − ½(−4.0)(3.0)² = 75 + 18

s = 93 m

Kinematics — when the five equations are illegal

average speed = total distance ÷ total time
You need: the whole journey, start to finish
It gives you: a single average figure
Reach for it when: the motion is not uniformly accelerated — stop-start journeys, several stages, changing acceleration
Note: this and its vector twin (average velocity = displacement ÷ total time) are the only kinematics tools that survive non-uniform motion.
Trap: you cannot use s = ut + ½at² on a multi-stage journey. Each stage needs its own equation, or you use averages across the whole thing.
Show an exampleHide the example

A runner covers 100 m in 12 s, rests for 8 s, then covers another 100 m in 14 s. Find the average speed for the whole run.

The acceleration is nowhere near uniform, so no suvat equation applies to the journey as a whole.

total distance = 200 m, total time = 12 + 8 + 14 = 34 s

average speed = 200 ÷ 34

≈ 5.9 m s⁻¹ — and note this is not the average of 8.33 and 7.14, because the rest counts as time.

gradient of a graph
You need: a displacement–time or velocity–time graph
It gives you: velocity from a d–t graph; acceleration from a v–t graph
Reach for it when: the question hands you a graph instead of numbers, or the line is curved
Note: a curved line means the quantity is changing, so take the gradient of the tangent at that instant.
Trap: gradient of a displacement–time graph is velocity, not acceleration. Going one step too far down the chain is a common slip.
Show an exampleHide the example

A velocity–time graph rises in a straight line from 5.0 m s⁻¹ at t = 2.0 s to 17 m s⁻¹ at t = 6.0 s. Find the acceleration.

Gradient of a v–t graph is acceleration.

a = Δv ÷ Δt = (17 − 5.0) ÷ (6.0 − 2.0) = 12 ÷ 4.0

a = 3.0 m s⁻²

area under a velocity–time graph
You need: a velocity–time graph
It gives you: displacement
Reach for it when: you need a distance and the acceleration is not uniform, so no suvat equation is legal
Note: split the shape into triangles and rectangles and add them.
Trap: area below the time axis counts as negative displacement. For total distance travelled, add the magnitudes; for displacement, subtract.
Show an exampleHide the example

A v–t graph shows a body accelerating from rest to 8.0 m s⁻¹ over the first 4.0 s, then holding 8.0 m s⁻¹ for 6.0 s. Find the total displacement.

Triangle: ½ × 4.0 × 8.0 = 16 m

Rectangle: 8.0 × 6.0 = 48 m

s = 16 + 48 = 64 m

Dynamics — forces, mass and weight

W = mg
You need: mass m in kg and g (10 N kg⁻¹ on Earth)
It gives you: weight in newtons
Reach for it when: the question gives a mass but an equation needs a force, or vice versa
Note: mass is measured on a balance and never changes; weight is a force and changes with g.
Trap: weight is in newtons, mass in kilograms. Writing “weight = 5 kg” loses the mark even if the number is right.
Show an exampleHide the example

A 0.60 kg book rests on a table. Find its weight, and its weight on the Moon where g = 1.6 N kg⁻¹.

On Earth: W = mg = 0.60 × 10 = 6.0 N

On the Moon: W = 0.60 × 1.6 = 0.96 N

6.0 N on Earth, 0.96 N on the Moon — but the mass is 0.60 kg in both places.

density = mass ÷ volume
You need: mass and volume of the same object
It gives you: density, in kg m⁻³ or g cm⁻³
Reach for it when: the question compares materials, asks whether something floats, or quotes a density to get a mass
Note: convert before you divide: 1.0 g cm⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³.
Trap: mixing units mid-calculation. Decide on g and cm³, or kg and m³, and stay there.
Show an exampleHide the example

A metal block measures 2.0 cm × 3.0 cm × 5.0 cm and has a mass of 240 g. Find its density in kg m⁻³.

Volume = 2.0 × 3.0 × 5.0 = 30 cm³

density = 240 ÷ 30 = 8.0 g cm⁻³

8.0 g cm⁻³ = 8000 kg m⁻³

FR = ma
You need: the resultant force and the mass
It gives you: acceleration — or the resultant force, if you already know a
Reach for it when: the forces on the body are unbalanced, so it speeds up, slows down or changes direction
Note: if the body moves at constant velocity or is stationary, a = 0, so FR = 0 and all the forces balance. That is often the whole question.
Trap: F must be the resultant, not one single force. Adding up the forces first is the step people skip.
Show an exampleHide the example

A 1200 kg car has a driving force of 4000 N and a total resistance of 1600 N. Find its acceleration.

Resultant first: FR = 4000 − 1600 = 2400 N

FR = ma → 2400 = 1200a

a = 2.0 m s⁻². Using 4000 N instead of 2400 N would have given 3.3 m s⁻², a wrong answer from correct algebra.

closed vector triangle
You need: exactly three forces on a body in equilibrium
It gives you: an unknown force’s size or direction
Reach for it when: a stationary object is held by three forces and you need one of them
Note: draw the three arrows head to tail; because they balance, the triangle closes. Then use scale drawing, or Pythagoras and trigonometry.
Trap: this is not a formula to memorise, it is a construction. “Equilibrium” and “three forces” together are the signal to draw, not to calculate.
Show an exampleHide the example

A lamp of weight 24 N hangs from two wires. What does the closed triangle tell you?

The weight acts straight down at 24 N. The two tensions must be drawn head to tail from the end of the weight vector back to its start.

Since the triangle closes, the vertical components of the two tensions add to 24 N, and their horizontal components cancel.

Set up those two statements and you can solve for either tension.

Work, energy and power

W = F × s
You need: a force and the distance moved in the direction of that force
It gives you: work done, in joules
Reach for it when: something is pushed, pulled, lifted or dragged through a distance
Note: if the displacement is perpendicular to the force, the work done by that force is zero.
Trap: carrying a box horizontally does no work against its weight, however tired you get. The weight points down, the movement is sideways.
Show an exampleHide the example

A 50 N box is lifted 1.1 m, then carried 2.0 m horizontally at constant speed. Find the work done against gravity in each stage.

Lifting: the force and the movement are both vertical, so W = 50 × 1.1 = 55 J.

Carrying: the weight is vertical, the movement is horizontal, so the vertical displacement is 0.

55 J lifting, 0 J carrying.

EK = ½mv²  ·  EP = mgh
You need: mass and speed, or mass and change in height
It gives you: energy in the kinetic or gravitational potential store
Reach for it when: the question asks how much energy something has, or has gained or lost
Note: h is measured from whatever reference level you choose — say what it is.
Trap: EK depends on v², so doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy. “Twice as fast” never means “twice the energy”.
Show an exampleHide the example

A 1500 kg car speeds up from 10 m s⁻¹ to 20 m s⁻¹. How much energy went into its kinetic store?

At 10 m s⁻¹: EK = ½(1500)(10)² = 75 000 J

At 20 m s⁻¹: EK = ½(1500)(20)² = 300 000 J

Gain = 225 kJ. Doubling the speed needed four times the energy, not two.

mgh = ½mv²
You need: a drop (or a rise) with no friction mentioned
It gives you: the speed at the bottom, or the height reached
Reach for it when: energy converts cleanly from one store to another — falling, sliding down a smooth ramp, swinging on a smooth pivot
Note: the mass appears on both sides, so it cancels. If the question gives you a mass and it vanishes, that is a sign you chose right.
Trap: the moment the question says “rough” or “friction”, this is no longer legal. Some energy has gone to the internal store of the surroundings.
Show an exampleHide the example

A 4.0 kg parcel slides down a smooth curved ramp from a height of 5.0 m. Take g = 10 m s⁻². Find its speed at the bottom.

Loss from the gravitational store = gain in the kinetic store.

mgh = ½mv² → the m cancels → (10)(5.0) = ½v² → v² = 100

v = 10 m s⁻¹, and the 4.0 kg was never needed — a favourite exam trick.

FR × s = ½mv² − ½mu²
You need: the resultant force, the distance, and both speeds
It gives you: whichever one of those is missing
Reach for it when: a force acts over a distance and you want the change in speed, without touching suvat
Note: this is the work–energy theorem: work done by the resultant force = change in kinetic store.
Trap: again the force must be the resultant. A braking question means the resultant points backwards, so the work done is negative.
Show an exampleHide the example

A 0.50 kg ball moving at 8.0 m s⁻¹ is stopped by a constant resistive force over 2.0 m. Find that force.

FR × s = ½mv² − ½mu² = 0 − ½(0.50)(8.0)² = −16 J

FR × 2.0 = −16

FR = −8.0 N — the minus sign says the force opposes the motion, which is exactly what a resistive force does.

P = W ÷ t
You need: energy transferred (or work done) and the time it took
It gives you: power, in watts
Reach for it when: the question quotes a job and how long it took — lifting a load in 12 s, a motor running for 3 minutes
Note: W here is energy in joules, and 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹.
Trap: this and P = Fv are the two power equations. Pick by what you are given: a time points here, a speed points to P = Fv.
Show an exampleHide the example

A crane lifts a 300 N crate through 8.0 m in 12 s. Find the useful output power.

Useful work done = F × s = 300 × 8.0 = 2400 J

P = W ÷ t = 2400 ÷ 12

P = 200 W

P = F × v
You need: a force and a speed, at the same moment
It gives you: power, in watts
Reach for it when: something moves at a steady speed against a resistance — a car cruising, a lift rising, a boat at constant velocity
Note: at constant velocity the resultant force is zero, so the driving force equals the total resistance. That is usually the hidden first step.
Trap: no time is given in these questions. If you find yourself inventing one so you can use P = W ÷ t, you have picked the wrong equation.
Show an exampleHide the example

A lift raises a 5000 N load at a steady 0.80 m s⁻¹. Find the power of the motor.

Steady speed → resultant force is zero → the tension equals the weight, 5000 N.

P = F × v = 5000 × 0.80

P = 4000 W = 4.0 kW. Going via EP = mgh then P = W ÷ t is correct physics but unusable — you were given a speed, not a time.

efficiency = (useful output ÷ total input) × 100%
You need: two energies (or two powers) — what went in, and what came out usefully
It gives you: a percentage
Reach for it when: the question mentions waste, losses, or how good a machine is
Note: total input = useful output + wasted energy, so if you are given any two of the three you can find the third.
Trap: decide carefully which number is the useful one. The energy the machine draws is always the input, never the output.
Show an exampleHide the example

An electric motor lifts a 10 N load through 5.0 m using 65 J of electrical energy. Find the efficiency and the energy wasted.

Useful output = work done on the load = 10 × 5.0 = 50 J

Total input = 65 J

efficiency = (50 ÷ 65) × 100%

77%, and 65 − 50 = 15 J wasted to the internal store of the surroundings.

The four mix-ups that cost the most marks

Mix-upHow to tell them apart
P = W ÷ t vs P = F × vLook at what the question gives you. A time sends you to P = W ÷ t. A steady speed sends you to P = Fv. Inventing the missing one is the error.
Using suvat when acceleration is not uniformCheck the v–t graph. Straight line → the five equations are legal. Curve, or several stages → use gradients, areas and averages instead.
F = ma with one force instead of the resultantAdd the forces up first, minding directions. Constant velocity or stationary means FR = 0, which is a statement, not a dead end.
mgh = ½mv² on a rough surfaceThe words “rough”, “friction” or “air resistance” break it. Energy has left to the internal store, so the two are no longer equal.
One last check before you write the answer. Does the unit match the quantity? Newtons for a force, joules for energy, watts for power, m s⁻² for acceleration. A wrong unit is often the first sign that the wrong equation went in at the top.

Worked Examples & Practice Debrief

The questions from your practices and worksheets, reduced to the method. If you can reproduce the first line of each one, the arithmetic follows.

1 · Two perpendicular forces Dynamics Practice Q1

A 4.0 N force acts due north on a 2.0 kg object at rest; a 3.0 N force pushes it due east.

Resultant force: the forces are perpendicular, so FR = √(4.0² + 3.0²) = 5.0 N, at an angle tan⁻¹(3.0/4.0) = 37° east of north.
(i) Acceleration: a = FR ÷ m = 5.0 ÷ 2.0 = 2.5 m s⁻², 37° east of north (same direction as the resultant force).
(ii) Velocity after 2.0 s: v = u + at = 0 + 2.5 × 2.0 = 5.0 m s⁻¹, also 37° east of north.
Marker's note: both answers are vectors — a magnitude alone will not score full marks.
2 · Velocity–time graph of a car Dynamics Practice Q3

A 1000 kg car speeds up from 0 to 5.0 m s⁻¹ in 5.0 s, cruises to 11.0 s, then decelerates. Road friction is 125 N.

(i) 0 – 5.0 s: a = gradient = 5.0 ÷ 5.0 = 1.0 m s⁻².
FR = ma → driving force − 125 = 1000 × 1.0 → driving force = 1125 N.
(ii) 5.0 – 11.0 s: constant velocity, so a = 0 and FR = 0.
driving force − 125 = 0 → driving force = 125 N.
The idea being tested: constant velocity does not mean no driving force — it means the driving force exactly balances friction.
3 · Two connected masses Dynamics Practice Q4

A 4.0 kg block is connected by a cable to a 2.0 kg block, which is pulled by a 20 N force. They move at a constant 3.0 m s⁻¹. Friction on the left block, F₁, is twice that on the right block, F₂.

Constant speed → a = 0 → resultant force on each block = 0. Take rightwards as positive.
Left block: T − F₁ = 0, so T = F₁ = 2F₂.
Right block: 20 − F₂ − T = 0, so T = 20 − F₂.
Solve: 2F₂ = 20 − F₂ → F₂ = 6.7 N, F₁ = 13 N, and the tension T = 13 N (2 s.f.).
4 · The school bag Dynamics Practice, O-Level Q10

A bag is pulled with force P against 0.5 N of friction; a graph of acceleration a against P is given, crossing the P-axis at 0.5 N.

(a) Why must P exceed 0.5 N? The applied force must be greater than the frictional force for the resultant force to be non-zero, so that the bag can accelerate.
(b)(ii) Finding m: at P = 2.0 N the resultant force = 2.0 − 0.5 = 1.5 N and the graph gives a = 0.75 m s⁻².
m = F ÷ a = 1.5 ÷ 0.75 = 2.0 kg. Do not take the gradient — the line does not pass through the origin, so a is not directly proportional to P.
(c)(i) v = u + at = 0 + 0.75 × 3.0 = 2.3 m s⁻¹.
(c)(ii) P reduced to 0.5 N: the resultant force becomes zero, so the acceleration is zero and the bag continues at a constant velocity of 2.3 m s⁻¹ (Newton's first law).
(d) Partner of P: the force acting on the student by the bag, equal in magnitude to P and opposite in direction.
5 · MRT carriages Worksheet 8 Q3

Two identical carriages move right at constant velocity; friction on each is 1.65 kN. The engine is in the right-hand (first) carriage.

Tension on the left carriage: net force = 0 → T − 1.65 = 0 → T = 1.65 kN.
Driving force: for the right carriage, −1.65 (tension) + driving force − 1.65 (friction) = 0 → 3.30 kN.
Accelerating case: with friction 2.00 kN each, mass 2000 kg each and a = 2 m s⁻², treat both carriages as one system:
driving force − 2 × 2000 = 4000 × 2.00 → driving force = 12 000 N.
General result for n carriages at constant velocity: driving force = nf, where f is the friction on one carriage.
6 · The Perseverance rover Worksheet 8 Q2

A 1000 kg rover is lowered at constant velocity onto Mars, where g = 3.721 m s⁻², by three ropes at equal angles.

Constant velocity → resultant force = 0. Total tension = weight = 1000 × 3.721 = 3721 N.
Per rope: 3721 ÷ 3 = 1240 N (4 s.f.).
Why a parachute helps: it increases the resistive force of air on the rover, creating a resultant force opposite to the motion, which reduces the acceleration of the descent. On a planet with no atmosphere it would do nothing, because there is no air to provide the resistive force.
If it were simply dropped from 25 m: v² = u² + 2as = 0 + 2(3.721)(25) → v = 14 m s⁻¹, which on impact would mean a force of order 10⁵ N — hence the ropes.
7 · The nail and the cork board WEP Practice Q1

A 10.5 g nail falls from rest through 80.0 cm and embeds 4.8 cm into a cork board.

(a) Would a heavier nail take longer? No — it takes the same time, because the acceleration due to gravity is independent of mass.
(b) Work done on the nail by the board. Total drop = 80.0 + 4.8 = 84.8 cm.
Loss in gravitational potential store = mgh = (0.0105)(10)(0.848) = 0.08904 J.
By conservation of energy the work done to stop the nail equals this loss → 0.089 J (2 s.f.).
(c) Average deceleration. W = Fd → F = 0.08904 ÷ 0.048 = 1.855 N.
a = F ÷ m = 1.855 ÷ 0.0105 = 180 m s⁻² (2 s.f.).
The trick: the height must include the 4.8 cm travelled inside the board, because the nail keeps falling while it decelerates.
8 · Car up an incline Worksheet 9 Q2

A 1500 kg car climbs to a height of 10.0 m on a 12.0° slope against 500 N of friction, with a driving force of 8.40 kN. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

(a) Gain in gravitational potential store: mgh = 1500 × 9.81 × 10.0 = 147 kJ.
(b) Energy transferred away by friction: slope length = 10.0 ÷ sin 12.0° = 48.097 m; W = Fs = 500 × 48.097 = 24 000 J.
(c) Speed at 10.0 m: work done by engine = Fs = 8400 × 48.097 = 404 kJ.
By conservation of energy: 404 010 = 147 000 + EK + 24 000 → EK = 233 010 J → ½(1500)v² = 233 010 → v = 17.6 m s⁻¹.
Common error: using F = ma with only the driving force. Along a slope the component of the weight also acts, so the energy route is safer.
9 · The bouncing nickel ball Worksheet 9 Q3

A nickel sphere of radius 2.00 cm (ρ = 8.908 g cm⁻³) falls from 50.0 cm and rebounds to 30.0 cm.

Mass: m = ρV = 8.908 × (4/3)π(2.00)³ = 298.51 g = 0.29851 kg. Convert to SI units before substituting.
Work done by the gravitational field: mgh = 0.29851 × 9.81 × 0.500 = 1.46 J (3 s.f.).
Percentage energy loss on impact: since both energies are mgh with the same m and g, the masses cancel:
loss = (1 − h₂/h₁) × 100% = (1 − 30.0/50.0) × 100% = 40%.
Plausible observation: a loud sound is heard on impact — some energy in the kinetic store is transferred away by sound waves, which is why the ball cannot return to its original height.
10 · Motor and friction WEP Practice Q2

A battery supplies 500 J to a motor that pulls an object 40.5 m at constant speed with a 6.00 N force.

(a) Efficiency: useful energy = Fs = 6.00 × 40.5 = 243 J → efficiency = (243 ÷ 500) × 100% = 48.6%.
(b) Frictional force: by conservation of energy the wasted 500 − 243 = 257 J is the work done against friction → F = 257 ÷ 40.5 = 6.35 N.
Spot the inconsistency: at constant speed the frictional force should equal the 6.00 N driving force. The mismatch tells you the question's numbers are slightly off — noticing this is exactly the physical reasoning being trained.
